author: Michael Loria
title: Former SPLC official arrested in federal case against civil rights group - NewsBreak
text:
By Michael Loria Aysha Bagchi ,
8 hours ago A former top official of a civil rights group targeted by the Department of Justice for allegedly funding the extremism they were supposed to dismantle has been arrested, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced.
Heidi L. Beirich, a former intelligence director at Southern Poverty Law Center, was arrested in California on Aug. 12 in connection with the federal government’s case against the anti-extremism group, the DOJ said in a statement . Blanche, speaking about the case at an unrelated news conference, said the 59-year-old furthered the organization’s alleged scheme by helping open bank accounts that funneled money back to extremist organizations.
Beirich's arrest is the latest in the DOJ's case against the civil rights group long seen as an essential foil to the Ku Klux Klan and which historically worked with federal authorities to build cases against extremists. DOJ leaders under President Donald Trump dismantled that partnership and in April first announced their case against the group.
According to federal prosecutors, the group took donations and used them to fund the extremist groups they had promised to dismantle. Leaders at the group slammed the accusations as "false." People familiar with the SPLC’s tactics have said the group used donations to pay informants within extremist groups, a tactic also used by the DOJ.
Heidi Beirich the Intelligence Project Director, Southern Poverty Law Center, during the Investigation Discovery portion of the Discovery Communications Winter TCA Event 2018 at the Langham Hotel on Jan. 12, 2018 in Pasadena, Calif. By Amanda Edwards, Getty Images for Discovery Michael J. Proctor, a lawyer for Beirich, said in a statement shared with USA TODAY that the Trump administration is using the justice system to silence opponents, and that his client is innocent.
"We believe the charges against her and the SPLC are politically motivated, and Dr. Beirich has been targeted in this case because of the important work she has done to combat hate groups and extremists," Proctor said. Beirich holds a PhD in political science from Purdue University.
"She welcomes the opportunity to present the truth in court," Proctor added.
What to know about the DOJ case In previous court filings, the DOJ alleged that the Southern Poverty Law Center committed wire fraud when it sought donations to dismantle violent extremist groups. The fundraising efforts were fraudulent, according to the DOJ, because the center allegedly didn't tell donors that some of the money would be used to pay high-level group leaders to be informants.
In a new charging document that adds Beirich as a criminal defendant in the case, the DOJ alleged that Beirich oversaw payments to informants, including to one with whom she had a romantic relationship.
The DOJ also specifically alleged that Beirich paid one extremist about $6,000 in donors' money to falsely take responsibility for stealing, copying and returning documents that belonged to an extremist group.
In reality, according to the document, the theft-and-return was carried out by the person with whom, for some period, Beirich allegedly had a romantic relationship. That person isn't named in the document.
Beirich used the copies for a story in the center's "Hatewatch" publication, which by its own description "monitors and exposes activities of the hard right in the United States."
Extremism in the US: Leaked documents expose growing White supremacist group
Alleged bank accounts scheme The new indictment also alleges Beirich participated along with the SPLC in a criminal conspiracy to conceal money laundering through how they paid informants.
Specifically, Beirich and other center employees allegedly transferred donated funds to bank accounts in the names of fictitious entities such as "Fox Photography" and "Tech Writers." They also allegedly masked direct payments to informants with similar names.
Part of what made that a crime, according to the charges, was that it was meant to hide the alleged criminal fraud against donors. Several former prosecutors previously told USA TODAY that means if the fraud case falls apart, the money laundering charge would, too.
"The money laundering allegation is entirely dependent upon there being a viable fraud allegation," said Stefan Cassella , a former federal prosecutor who focused on asset forfeiture and money laundering.
SPLC responds, experts question DOJ case Abbe Lowell, a lawyer for the SPLC, called the DOJ's latest set of accusations against the group "legally and factually flawed."
"This charge reflects a desperate government confronting a weak case, scrambling to make something – anything – stick as we approach trial," Lowell told USA TODAY. "The SPLC did not lie to donors, did not mislead the banks it did business with, and its informant program prevented violence and saved lives."
In a separate statement shared with USA TODAY, the SPLC said its work would continue.
"Taking on violent hate and extremist groups is among the most dangerous work there is, and we believe it is also among the most important work we do. The actions taken by the DOJ will not shake our resolve," the statement said. "We remain steadfast in our fight for justice and in our commitment to ensuring the promise of the Civil Rights movement becomes a reality for all."
Some legal experts have questioned the strength of the DOJ's fraud case against the law center, given that paying for information on extremist groups is arguably helpful to combatting those groups.
"Paying informants to then dismantle the organization seems like something that people would expect to be one of the tactics that are used, so that seems like a very weak case to me," Amy Markopoulos, a former federal prosecutor who spent years in the DOJ's fraud section, previously told USA TODAY.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Former SPLC official arrested in federal case against civil rights group
